title: Customers Who Purchased from Every Category
description: Find customers who have purchased at least one product from **every product category**. This is a classic **relational division** problem — compare each customer's distinct category coverage to the total number of categories.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE orders (order_id INT, customer_id INT, product_id INT); CREATE TABLE products (product_id INT, name VARCHAR(100), category VARCHAR(50)); INSERT INTO products VALUES (1,'Laptop','Electronics'),(2,'Phone','Electronics'),(3,'Shirt','Clothing'),(4,'Pants','Clothing'),(5,'Hammer','Hardware'); INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,1,1),(2,1,3),(3,2,1),(4,2,3),(5,2,5),(6,3,1),(7,3,2),(8,4,3),(9,4,4),(10,4,5),(11,5,2),(12,5,4),(13,5,5);
solution_sql: SELECT o.customer_id FROM orders o JOIN products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id GROUP BY o.customer_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT p.category) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT category) FROM products) ORDER BY o.customer_id

test_cases.description: 3 categories total (Electronics, Clothing, Hardware). Customer 2 (Elec+Cloth+Hardware) and Customer 5 (Elec+Cloth+Hardware) qualify. Customers 1, 3, 4 are missing at least one category.

hints: Count the number of DISTINCT categories a customer has bought from using COUNT(DISTINCT p.category) after joining orders with products.
Compare that count to the total number of categories with a subquery: HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT p.category) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT category) FROM products).
explanation: Relational division: find customers whose category coverage equals the full set. There are 3 categories. Customer 1: Electronics+Clothing only (2/3) ✗. Customer 2: products 1(Elec)+3(Cloth)+5(Hardware) = all 3 ✓. Customer 3: Electronics only (1/3) ✗. Customer 4: products 3(Cloth)+4(Cloth)+5(Hardware) = 2 categories ✗. Customer 5: products 2(Elec)+4(Cloth)+5(Hardware) = all 3 ✓. Result: customers 2 and 5.
